errors.problem: The tap gloss for مُدَرِّسَة says 'school'. مُدَرِّسَة is 'teacher (f)'; 'school' is مَدْرَسَة. This is the correct answer of d8q2 ('How do you say a female teacher?'), so a learner who taps the right answer is told it means 'school' and will either pick a wrong option or learn the wrong word.
errors.alsoChange: the dictionary/tap entry for مُدَرِّسَة wherever it is defined, so every occurrence is corrected

errors.problem: In the intro list 'New letters: ف ق ك ل' and in quiz d6q5 ('Which letter is the deep k?') the four options are letters, but tapping ل gives the preposition gloss 'for; belonging to' instead of 'the letter lām' (the other three give 'the letter fāʾ/qāf/kāf'). A beginner learning the alphabet is told lām 'means' for.
errors.alsoChange: keep the preposition sense for the prefixed لِـ in words; only the standalone letter in letter lists/letter quizzes needs the letter-name gloss

errors.problem: In 'Today you finish the alphabet: م ن ه و ي' the tap gloss for و is the conjunction 'and' while the neighbours are 'the letter mīm/nūn/hāʾ/yāʾ'. In a letter list the learner needs 'the letter wāw'.
errors.alsoChange: same standalone-letter rule as for ل on day 6

errors.current: أَنْتَ=you (written without vowel marks: anta or anti)
errors.problem: The tap gloss for أَنْتَ and أَنْتِ says the word is 'written without vowel marks: anta or anti', but every occurrence in the course is fully vocalised (أَنْتَ with fatḥa = anta, to a man; أَنْتِ with kasra = anti, to a woman). The gloss contradicts the lesson of day 2 ('Arabic has two words for you') and the segs on the same lines ('you (to a man)' / 'you (to a woman)'). In quiz d2q3 the learner is asked what أَنْتَ means and the tap tells them it is ambiguous. The same wrong text appears for أَنْتِ (أَنْتِ=you (written without vowel marks: anta or anti)).
errors.fix: أَنْتَ=you (to a man) and أَنْتِ=you (to a woman)
errors.alsoChange: the shared dictionary entries for أَنْتَ and أَنْتِ, so the tap gloss matches the segs everywhere

errors.current: Min Amrīkā Walubnān Wamiṣr wabilād ukhrā
errors.problem: Engine: when وَ is prefixed to a capitalised proper name the transliteration capitalises the whole token mid-sentence and drops the hyphen: 'Walubnān Wamiṣr' (day 3 l10 and day 8 reading), 'Wasāmī' (day 3 l4), while elsewhere the same prefix is rendered 'wa-anā', 'Wa-l-ustādh', 'wa-ummī'. The Arabic is correct; the output should read 'wa-Lubnān wa-Miṣr', 'wa-Sāmī'.
errors.fix: render clitic وَ before a proper name as 'wa-' + capitalised name (wa-Lubnān, wa-Miṣr, wa-Sāmī), lower-case unless sentence-initial
errors.alsoChange: nothing in the content files; transliteration engine only

notes.note: تَعْبَان is the everyday (Egyptian/Levantine) word for 'tired'; the fuṣḥā adjectives are مُتْعَب or تَعِب. Not wrong for a polite everyday dialogue, but as the only word for 'tired' taught in week 1 the owner may want مُتْعَب shown alongside.
'I really love the Arabic language' adds 'really'; the Arabic أَنَا أُحِبُّ اللُّغَة الْعَرَبِيَّة is simply 'I love the Arabic language'.

English says 'my bag is new too' but the Arabic is وَالْحَقِيبَة جَدِيدَة ('and the bag is new too'). Context makes it her bag, but the seg gloss shows 'the bag'; either 'the bag' in the English or حَقِيبَتِي in the Arabic would align them.
'Welcome to our class' for أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا فِي الصَّفّ ('in the class'); harmless, but segs say 'the class'.

Culture fact: 'In America the week starts on Monday' — US calendars conventionally start the week on Sunday; it is the working week that starts on Monday. Consider 'the working week starts on Monday'.
Culture fact: Lebanon (part of the Levant) mostly uses the Western digits 0123456789, like North Africa; 'the Levant' as a whole is an over-generalisation.

'the l of the article is silent / not pronounced' before a sun letter is a teaching simplification: the lām is assimilated to the following consonant, which is then doubled (as-sayyāra, as-sabt). Fine for beginners; a one-line hint that the next letter is doubled would help.
هَاتِفِي بِدُونِ بَطَّارِيَّة الْيَوْم ('my phone is without battery') is understandable but unidiomatic; بَطَّارِيَّةُ هَاتِفِي فَارِغَة or هَاتِفِي مُغْلَق would be more natural MSA.

مَصْر (Maṣr) with fatḥa is the Egyptian colloquial pronunciation and the note says so; fine, but the learner has just learnt مِصْر — consider writing both forms side by side so the vowel difference is explicit.

notes.path: all intro/why lines that mention the letter ة or ا
notes.note: In transliterated prose the engine renders the standalone letter ة as 'A / at' and ا as 'Ā / ʾ' (e.g. 'add A / at for a feminine noun', 'four letters: Ā / ʾ b t th'). Correct but hard to read; rendering the letter name (tāʾ marbūṭa, alif) in prose would be clearer.

Hyphenation after the clitic وَ is inconsistent: 'wa-anā', 'wa-ummī', 'Wa-l-ustādh' but 'wahuwa', 'washukran', 'wamutarjim', 'wajamīla'. A single rule (always 'wa-') would be easier for beginners to parse.

summary: Read all 2,490 lines of audit/days-01-10.txt (days 1–10: titles, intros, objectives, real-life stories, sentences with literals and mistakes, dialogues, readings, quizzes and completions). Checked every Arabic string for spelling, harakat, case endings, hamza seats, tāʾ marbūṭa, agreement (gender, number, definiteness), verb forms and imperatives, iḍāfa and number constructions, the English translations and literals, every seg and tap gloss, every quiz answer key and the generated transliteration. The Arabic itself is clean: I found no misspelt word, no agreement or case error, no wrong verb form and no wrong quiz answer key; number phrases (ثَلَاثَة إِخْوَة, عَشَرَة أَسْئِلَة, سَبْعَة أَيَّام), time expressions (إِلَّا رُبْعًا), iḍāfa forms and the imperatives (اِشْتَرِ, اُدْرُسْ, اِفْتَحُوا, تَعَالَوْا) are all correct MSA. The errors are all in the tap-gloss layer: one major (مُدَرِّسَة glossed 'school' on the correct answer of d8q2) and three minor dictionary glosses that show the wrong sense in context (ل and و glossed as the preposition/conjunction inside letter lists and a letter quiz; أَنْتَ/أَنْتِ glossed as 'written without vowel marks' although fully vocalised, in nine places), plus one minor engine issue (capitalised 'Walubnān Wamiṣr' after the clitic وَ). Eleven notes cover register (تَعْبَان), small translation drift (really / my bag / our class), two culture facts (US week start, Levant digits), the 'silent lām' simplification and transliteration readability. Totals: 1 major, 4 minor, 11 notes.
